inlines.text: Class 8C sit tests in English, Maths and Science. The table shows some summary information about their results.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Assuming the marks use comparable scales, in which subject did students do best by median mark?

answer.worked: Maths has the highest median mark: $61$ marks, compared with $59$ for Science and $56$ for English. Students did best in Maths by median mark.

children.label: b
children.prompt: In which subject were the students' marks most similar?

answer.worked: Science has the smallest range: $22$ marks, compared with $35$ for English and $47$ for Maths. Its marks are therefore the most similar by this measure.

inlines.text: Here are the heights of five basketball players.
Here are the heights of six gymnasts.
Discuss what you notice about the median height of the basketball players compared to the median height of the gymnasts. Explain why this might be the case.
Greater height can help with reaching the basket or taking rebounds, which may explain the taller basketball players in these samples.

answer.worked:
Basketball heights in ascending order (cm): $194,\ 195,\ \underline{197},\ 200,\ 201$.

There are five values, so the third value is the middle value. The basketball players’ median height is $197\,\text{cm}$.

Gymnast heights in ascending order (cm): $146,\ 152,\ \underline{154},\ \underline{158},\ 158,\ 160$.

There are six values, so find the mean of the third and fourth values.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Gymnast median}&=\frac{154+158}{2}\,\text{cm}\\\text{Gymnast median}&=156\,\text{cm}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\text{Difference}&=(197-156)\,\text{cm}\\\text{Difference}&=41\,\text{cm}\end{align*}$$

The basketball players’ median height is $41\,\text{cm}$ greater. Greater height can give an advantage when reaching the basket or taking rebounds. This is a possible reason for the taller basketball players in these samples.

content.prompt: Compare the range, mean, mode, and median of these two datasets.

children.prompt: Range:

answer.worked:
Range is the greatest value minus the least value.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Male range}&=36-27\\\text{Male range}&=9\text{ min}\\\text{Female range}&=34-27\\\text{Female range}&=7\text{ min}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Mean:

answer.worked:
Mean is the total divided by the number of data values. Each dot represents one time.

Male: $40$ dots.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Total}&=4\times27+3\times28+4\times29+4\times30+5\times31+3\times32+4\times33+4\times34+6\times35+3\times36\\\text{Total}&=1265\text{ min}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{1265}{40}\\\bar{x}&=31.625\text{ min}\end{align*}$$

Female: $30$ dots.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Total}&=5\times27+7\times28+7\times29+4\times30+3\times31+1\times32+2\times33+1\times34\\\text{Total}&=879\text{ min}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{879}{30}\\\bar{x}&=29.3\text{ min}\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Mode:

answer.short: Mode: Male: $35$ min; Female: $28$ and $29$ min.
answer.worked:
The mode is the value with the greatest frequency.

Male: $35$ min occurs $6$ times, more often than any other value.

Female: $28$ min and $29$ min each occur $7$ times, so both are modes.

children.prompt: Median:

answer.worked:
Read the dots in ascending order along the horizontal axis.

Male: $40$ values.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Position}&=\frac{40+1}{2}\\\text{Position}&=20.5\end{align*}$$

There are $20$ values at or below $31$. The 20th value is $31$ and the 21st value is $32$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Median}&=\frac{31+32}{2}\\\text{Median}&=31.5\text{ min}\end{align*}$$

Female: $30$ values.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Position}&=\frac{30+1}{2}\\\text{Position}&=15.5\end{align*}$$

There are $12$ values below $29$ and $19$ values at or below $29$. The 15th and 16th values are both $29$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Median}&=\frac{29+29}{2}\\\text{Median}&=29\text{ min}\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Boys are taller on average, with a higher mean and median.
Girls’ heights are more spread out with a higher range.

answer.worked:
There are $15$ boys and $18$ girls. Their total heights are $2301$ cm and $2585$ cm, respectively.

$$\begin{align*}\bar{x}_{\text{boys}}&=\frac{2301}{15}\text{ cm}\\\bar{x}_{\text{boys}}&=153.4\text{ cm}\\\bar{x}_{\text{girls}}&=\frac{2585}{18}\text{ cm}\\\bar{x}_{\text{girls}}&=143\frac{11}{18}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\text{Boys' median position}&=\frac{15+1}{2}\\\text{Boys' median position}&=8\\\text{Girls' median position}&=\frac{18+1}{2}\\\text{Girls' median position}&=9.5\end{align*}$$

The boys’ eighth height is $152$ cm. The girls’ ninth and tenth heights are $144$ cm and $145$ cm.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Boys' median}&=152\text{ cm}\\\text{Girls' median}&=\frac{144+145}{2}\text{ cm}\\\text{Girls' median}&=144.5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\text{Boys' range}&=(168-138)\text{ cm}\\\text{Boys' range}&=30\text{ cm}\\\text{Girls' range}&=(173-121)\text{ cm}\\\text{Girls' range}&=52\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

In these datasets, boys are taller on average because their mean and median are higher. Girls’ heights are more spread out because their range is larger.

inlines.text: The heights of students in a school netball team were measured and recorded as

inlines.latex: 166\text{ cm},\ 170\text{ cm},\ 168\text{ cm},\ 67\text{ cm},\ 170\text{ cm},\ 169\text{ cm}

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the mean, median and mode of this data.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Mean}&=\frac{166+170+168+67+170+169}{6}\\\text{Mean}&=\frac{910}{6}\\\text{Mean}&=151\frac{2}{3}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

This is approximately $151.67\text{ cm}$ to two decimal places.

Ordered heights: $67,\ 166,\ 168,\ 169,\ 170,\ 170\text{ cm}$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Median}&=\frac{168+169}{2}\\\text{Median}&=168.5\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

The most frequent height is $170\text{ cm}$, so the mode is $170\text{ cm}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Identify the outlier in this set of data.

answer.worked: The outlier is $67\text{ cm}$ because it is much smaller than the other heights, which are between $166\text{ cm}$ and $170\text{ cm}$.

inlines.text: Ignore the outlier and calculate the mean, median and mode of the remaining 5 heights.
Comment on how the summary statistics have changed.
The mean increases considerably, the median increases by

answer.worked:
Remaining heights in order: $166,\ 168,\ 169,\ 170,\ 170\text{ cm}$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Mean}&=\frac{166+168+169+170+170}{5}\\\text{Mean}&=\frac{843}{5}\\\text{Mean}&=168.6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

The middle height is $169\text{ cm}$, so the median is $169\text{ cm}$. The most frequent height is $170\text{ cm}$, so the mode is $170\text{ cm}$.

The mean increases considerably, from $151\frac{2}{3}\text{ cm}$ to $168.6\text{ cm}$. The median increases from $168.5\text{ cm}$ to $169\text{ cm}$, a rise of $0.5\text{ cm}$. The mode is unchanged.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Should the outlier be removed from the dataset in this case? Explain what you would check first.

inlines.text: Check the record or measurement first. Remove or correct
only if an error is confirmed; keep a genuine team member’s measurement.

answer.worked: Check the original record and remeasure the student if possible. Although $67\text{ cm}$ is unusual compared with the other heights, this alone does not prove an error. Correct a verified recording error; exclude the observation only if it is confirmed invalid or belongs to someone outside the intended group. Retain the measurement if it is genuine.

inlines.text: The mean of each dataset is shown below.
For which dataset is the mean a poor measure of a typical value because of a single outlier?

answer.worked:
The value $25$ is a single high outlier compared with $3,4,5,6,7$.

$$\begin{align*}\bar{x}&=\frac{3+4+5+6+7+25}{6}\\\bar{x}&=\frac{25}{3}\end{align*}$$

The outlier raises the mean above all five values in the cluster from $3$ to $7$.

Correct answer: C.

inlines.text: Which of the following is a limitation of the median as a measure of centre?
It does not take into account the precise value of each piece of data and so does not use all the information available in the data.
It cannot be used with data sets that contain negative numbers.
It cannot be used with datasets that have an even number of values.

answer.worked:
The median uses the middle value, or the mean of the two middle values, after the data are ordered. It does not use the precise magnitude of every value.

Correct answer: A.

inlines.text: For which dataset is the mode not a good average to use?

answer.worked:
For C, $1$ occurs twice; $7$, $8$ and $9$ each occur once. The mode is $1$, at the low end of the dataset, while most observations are $7$, $8$ and $9$.

Correct answer: C.

answer.short: Yes. Women’s ages cluster in the 50s and 60s and are negatively skewed; men’s ages cluster in the 40s and are positively skewed.
answer.worked: Read each stem as tens and each leaf as units. The women’s ages cluster in their 50s and 60s, with a tail towards younger ages, so their distribution is negatively skewed. The men’s ages cluster in their 40s, with a tail towards older ages, so their distribution is positively skewed. The women’s cluster is at higher ages, so Pat is correct.

content.prompt: Determine whether the intended survey design in each scenario is a census or a sample.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Everyone in the house getting to vote on which board game to play next.

answer.worked: Census. Everyone in the house is included, so the whole population is surveyed.

children.label: b
children.prompt: A scientist gathering 500g of soil to analyse land quality in the area.

answer.worked: Sample. The 500 g collected is only part of the soil in the area.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Every second shopper at a supermarket is asked if they like a product.

answer.worked: Sample. Asking every second shopper includes only part of the supermarket's shoppers.

children.label: d
children.prompt: A referendum where everyone in a country votes on a new law change.

answer.worked: Census. Under the stated scenario, everyone in the country votes, so the whole population is included.

children.label: e
children.prompt: A shop owner uses an automatic entrance counter to record every customer entry each day.

answer.worked: Census. The population is all customer entries that day, and every entry is counted.

inlines.text: A school conducts a survey to gather feedback on the quality of lunches.
They distribute the survey to every student in the school.

answer.worked: Census (intended design). Every student is offered the survey, so this is an attempted census. Complete response is not stated.

inlines.text: A polling agency conducts a survey to predict election outcomes.
They randomly select 5,000 voters across the country and gather their voting preferences.

answer.worked: Sample. The selected 5,000 voters are only part of the country's voters.

children.label: h
children.prompt: A company conducts a survey to gather feedback from all its employees about their satisfaction with the workplace environment.

answer.worked: Census. All the company's employees are included, so feedback is collected from the whole population.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Researchers conduct a survey to understand the prevalence of a specific health condition in a city. They randomly select households to participate in the survey.

answer.worked: Sample. Only selected households participate, so the survey covers part of the city's population.

children.label: j
children.prompt: A retail store sends out a survey to everyone who made a purchase in the past month to gauge their satisfaction with the store's services.

answer.worked: Census (intended design). Everyone who purchased in the past month is offered the survey, so this is an attempted census. Complete response is not stated.

inlines.text: Sampling bias occurs when the selection method systematically favours some members or views of the population. A sample may also be unrepresentative by chance.
Sources of sampling bias and other sampling limitations:
The selected group misrepresents the population.
Measuring average height of 15-year-olds by only surveying the basketball team.
A small sample may miss population variety and give results that vary greatly by chance. Small size alone does not make a sampling method biased.
Surveying only three people about a new highway.
The sampling method relies on people volunteering to participate.
A study on dietary habits attracting only health-conscious volunteers.
Considers only successful cases, ignoring failures.
Evaluating the success of businesses only by looking at those still in operation, ignoring those that have failed.

inlines.text: A survey was conducted to determine the average income of residents in a particular city. The survey only included responses from residents who lived in wealthy harbourside neighbourhoods.

answer.worked: Selection bias. Wealthy harbourside neighbourhoods do not represent residents across the whole city, so the city's average income is likely to be overestimated.

inlines.text: Mr Ding wants to know the percentage of school students who have maths as their favourite subject.
He surveys the Year 12 Maths Extension class.

answer.worked: Selection bias. Year 12 Maths Extension students are likely to be more interested in maths than school students generally, so the percentage choosing maths as their favourite subject is likely to be overestimated.

inlines.text: The government wanted to know farmers’ opinions on a new road.
They asked 2 farmers out of a community of 500.

answer.short: Small sample size; size alone does not establish bias.
answer.worked: Only 2 of 500 farmers were surveyed, so the sample may miss many opinions and its results may vary greatly by chance. Small size alone does not establish systematic bias; the selection method is not stated.

inlines.text: Investigating the religious beliefs of Australians by surveying people at shopping centres on Sunday mornings.

answer.worked: Selection bias. Sunday-morning shopping-centre visitors do not represent all Australians. People attending religious services at that time may be underrepresented.

content.prompt: Discuss why the following sampling methods may result in an unrepresentative sample:

children.label: a
children.prompt: Responses to a survey conducted by email.

inlines.text: only those with internet access respond; excludes people without email.

answer.worked: Selection bias: people without email access are excluded, so their views are not represented. Volunteer bias may also occur if those who choose to reply have different views from those who do not.

inlines.text: A survey on household spending is needed.
You take a random sample of a Sydney harbour-side suburb.
If the target is all Australian households, one harbour-side suburb may differ in income and spending; random sampling within it does not cover other areas.

answer.worked: If the target is all Australian households, households outside this suburb are excluded and may have different incomes and spending. Random selection within the suburb does not remove this selection bias.

children.label: c
children.prompt: A survey of the number of people who can touch their toes is done with students from a gymnastics class.

inlines.text: Gymnastics students are likely to be more flexible than people generally, so the proportion able to touch their toes may be overestimated.

answer.worked: For the wider population, this creates selection bias: gymnastics students are likely to be more flexible. The sample may therefore overestimate the proportion who can touch their toes.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Researching favourite music genres by interviewing people outside a classical music concert.

inlines.text: Classical-concert attendees may be more interested in classical music than the wider population.

answer.worked: If the target is the wider population, concert attendees may overrepresent people who favour classical music. Selecting respondents at this location can therefore create selection bias.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Finding opinions on new cycle lanes by interviewing members of the local cycling club.

inlines.text: Cycling-club members may be more likely to use and support cycle lanes than other residents.

answer.worked: If the target is all local residents, interviewing only cycling-club members creates selection bias. Their greater likely use of cycle lanes may lead to an overestimate of support.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Looking at the state of the economy by interviewing wealthy landowners.

inlines.text: Wealthy landowners don't represent the economic situation of all citizens.

answer.worked: Selection bias: wealthy landowners have different financial circumstances from many other citizens. Their experiences alone may give a distorted picture of the wider economy.

children.label: g
children.prompt: Researching favourite films of teenagers by interviewing teenage attendees at an anime convention.

inlines.text: Teenage anime-convention attendees may favour anime more than teenagers generally.

answer.worked: Selection bias: teenage convention attendees are likely to have a stronger interest in anime than teenagers generally. The sample may therefore overrepresent preferences for anime films.

children.label: h
children.prompt: A peak hour survey of the people on a train about whether they are employed.

inlines.text: If the aim is to represent the wider population, peak-hour train travellers may overrepresent people commuting to work.

answer.worked: If the target is the wider population, peak hour train passengers may include a higher proportion of employed commuters. This selection bias may overestimate the population's employment rate.

children.label: i
children.prompt: A survey at the train station of how Australians get to work.

inlines.text: Train-station sampling overrepresents train users and may miss many people who drive, use other transport or work from home.

answer.worked: Selection bias: sampling at a train station overrepresents train users and misses many other workers. Train travel may appear more common than it is among Australian workers.

children.label: j
children.prompt: A survey of the people in your year level on Australia’s most popular television shows

inlines.text: Your year level's preferences don't represent all Australians' viewing habits.

answer.worked: Selection bias: one year level represents a narrow age group and excludes Australians of other ages. Their television preferences may differ, so the sample may not represent Australia as a whole.

children.label: k
children.prompt: Year 7 students are interviewed about whether they like changes to the school uniform.

inlines.text: If the aim is to represent the whole school, interviewing only Year 7 excludes other year levels, whose opinions may differ.

answer.worked: If the target is all students at the school, interviewing only Year 7 creates selection bias. Other year levels are excluded and may have different opinions about the uniform changes.

children.label: l
children.prompt: Motorists stopped in peak hour are interviewed about traffic problems

inlines.text: If the aim is motorists generally, peak-hour interviews may overrepresent experiences of heavy congestion.

answer.worked: If the target is motorists generally, surveying only in peak hour creates selection bias. These motorists may experience heavier congestion than those travelling at other times.

children.label: m
children.prompt: A YouTuber asks their subscribers for feedback on their videos.

inlines.text: If the aim is all viewers, subscribers may be more engaged or favourable. Non-subscribers are omitted, and volunteers may differ from people who do not reply.

answer.worked: If the target is all viewers, asking only subscribers creates selection bias: non-subscribers are excluded, and subscribers may be more engaged or favourable. Volunteer bias may also occur if respondents differ from those who do not reply.

children.label: n
children.prompt: Triple J (pop rock station) radio listeners were asked to vote for the best song of the year.

inlines.text: If the aim is all music listeners, one station’s audience may have different preferences. Voluntary voters may also differ from non-voters.

answer.worked: If the target is all music listeners, selecting one station's audience creates selection bias because their tastes may differ from those of other listeners. Volunteer bias may also occur because only listeners who choose to vote are counted.

content.prompt: Describe why these questions may lead to a biased statistical investigation.

No negative rating is offered, so respondents cannot report a poor experience accurately.

answer.worked: There are not enough choices. “Excellent”, “Good” and “Satisfactory” are all satisfactory or better. A respondent who had a poor experience has no suitable negative option, so the results may appear too favourable.

inlines.text: How much do you spend on music?
No timeframe is stated; £10 and £20 have unclear categories; amounts below £5 or above £30 have no option.

answer.worked: The question is ambiguous because it does not specify a spending period, such as a week or a month. The ranges do not explain which category includes exactly £10 or £20. There are also not enough choices: spending below £5 or above £30 cannot be reported. Respondents may answer using different periods or be unable to choose a suitable category.

inlines.text: How would you rate the overall quality of service provided by our airline staff?
There are not enough choices: no neutral or intermediate rating is offered.

answer.worked: Only “Good” and “Poor” are offered. Someone with a neutral or intermediate opinion cannot report it accurately and must choose an unsuitable category or leave the question unanswered.

inlines.text: Write a criticism for the question and the
How often do you eat fast food?

entries.description:
In WW2, the US military found that returning planes were hit in these locations.
A statistician suggested that extra armour be placed at the places where the plane was not hit.

entries.expectedAnswer: The sample contains only planes that survived and returned; planes that failed to return are missing. The marked locations show damage that returning planes could survive. Hits in areas with few or no marks on returning planes, such as the engines or cockpit, may have been more likely to prevent a plane from returning. Extra armour should therefore protect those vulnerable areas. Method: apply page 89's definition of survivorship bias by identifying the surviving cases included and the failures excluded.
